These observations support the concept that early-stage MSA is characterised by diverse and often prominent non-motor manifestations. However, neurodegeneration in MSA variably involves the striatonigral, olivopontocerebellar, and autonomic systems, and some patients show involvement of only one or two systems in the early stage. In fact, 9% of patients with MSA do not exhibit autonomic dysfunction at any point during the disease course [ ]. Furthermore, other parkinsonian disorders, including Parkinson’s disease and progressive supranuclear palsy, can clinically masquerade as MSA during life, as these patients can also exhibit parkinsonism with severe autonomic dysfunction [ ]. Conversely, up to half of patients with early-stage MSA show a favourable response to L-DOPA, reflecting relatively mild neurodegeneration in the putamen [ , ]. Distinguishing such cases from Parkinson’s disease is therefore difficult, particularly in the absence of cerebellar ataxia and/or marked autonomic failure [ ]. Compounding this challenge, RBD is not specific to MSA or Lewy body diseases: it can also be caused by progressive supranuclear palsy, narcolepsy, the use of antidepressants, alcohol abuse, and various autoimmune diseases, including limbic encephalitis, anti-IgLON5 antibody–associated disease, multiple sclerosis, and Guillain–Barré syndrome [ , ]. Taken together, these factors underscore that an accurate clinical diagnosis of MSA at an early stage remains challenging when based solely on the constellation of clinical signs and symptoms. The development of reliable biomarkers for early-stage MSA is an urgent, unmet need. 5. Pathological and Molecular Alterations in the Early Stage of MSA In the literature, a number of terms are employed to describe the early stage of MSA, including “preclinical” and “early.” However, these terms do not necessarily refer to the same stage or timing of disease progression. Furthermore, the misconception persists that “minimal change” MSA represents an early stage of the disease. However, this type represents a rare variant of MSA rather than a specific disease stage. In this section, we describe the pathological and molecular changes that characterise each stage and type of MSA. 5.1. Preclinical MSA As of 2025, only six autopsy cases of preclinical MSA have been reported. All these reports primarily focused on neuropathological features, including the extent and distribution of neuronal loss, gliosis, and the occurrence of GCIs and NCIs [ , , , , ], and no studies have specifically investigated molecular alterations in preclinical MSA. Among the six autopsy cases, two showed no neuronal loss in the brain, whereas the remaining four exhibited mild neuronal loss within the striatonigral system. Notably, in all cases, GCIs were consistently and widely distributed throughout both the striatonigral and olivopontocerebellar systems [ , , , , ]. Thus, α-Syn accumulation precedes overt neurodegeneration. In three cases, most of the NCIs were located in the perinuclear region ( a), whereas NNIs were frequently observed along the inner surface of the nuclear membrane ( b) [ , , ]. Furthermore, Wiseman et al. reported that α-Syn fibrils within neurones penetrate the nuclear envelope, leading to its disruption and subsequent neuronal death [ ]. These findings suggest that the accumulation of α-Syn adjacent to the neuronal nucleus may represent one of the earliest pathogenic events in MSA. In addition, the precise initiation site of α-Syn accumulation within the central nervous system (CNS) remains unclear. Recently, Endo et al. developed α-Syn-specific positron emission tomography tracers that may enable in vivo detection of early α-Syn pathology [ ]. Further studies are warranted to determine the initial site of α-Syn pathology and to elucidate how it ultimately contributes to neurodegeneration in MSA. 5.2. Early-Stage MSA The term “early-stage” MSA has not been clearly defined. In this review, following previous reports [ , , ], early-stage MSA was defined as the period within 3 years of disease onset. At this stage, varying degrees of neurodegeneration can be observed in the striatonigral, olivopontocerebellar, and autonomic systems. CSF levels of parkinsonism-associated deglycase, tau, myelin basic protein (MBP), and neurofilament light chain (NfL), which reflect neurodegeneration in the brain, were significantly higher in patients with MSA than in those with Parkinson’s disease [ , , ]. In contrast, the plasma levels of miR-671-5p , implicated in neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis [ , ] differed between MSA-P and MSA-C [ ], suggesting that these miRNAs may aid in differentiating early-stage MSA-P and MSA-C. Furthermore, plasma homocysteine, an intermediate amino acid generated during methionine metabolism, is elevated in individuals with early-stage MSA compared with that in healthy controls [ ]. Homocysteine exerts neuronal toxicity by increasing oxidative injury in neurones and stimulating N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors [ , , ]; hence, increased methionine levels may contribute to neuronal degeneration in early-stage MSA. Recently, we isolated and compared extracellular vesicles from the CSF of individuals with Parkinson’s disease and those with early-stage MSA-P. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed significantly altered levels of transcripts ( RN7SL3 , RN7SL1 , miR19B2 , SYF2P2 , and S100A7 ) and proteins (psoriasin [S100A7] and dystroglycan 1) in patients with MSA-P compared with those with Parkinson’s disease. Although the roles of these transcripts and proteins in the early pathogenesis of MSA remain unclear, these transcriptomic and proteomic signatures may help identify early-stage MSA-P [ ]. Collectively, these findings indicate characteristic alterations in protein, cytokine, miRNA, and metabolite levels during the early stages of MSA. In contrast, “minimal change” MSA represents an atypical pathological variant characterised by neuronal loss restricted to specific regions with an otherwise typical distribution of GCIs [ , , , , , ]. To date, nine autopsy cases with minimal changes in MSA have been reported [ , , , , ]. The initially described affected regions were the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus [ , , , ]. Compared with typical MSA, patients with “minimal change” MSA showed a greater burden of NCIs, but not GCIs, in the caudate and substantia nigra [ ]. However, subsequent reports documented cases in which neuronal loss was restricted to the olivopontocerebellar system [ ] or limbic system [ ]. These cases were likewise classified as “minimal change” MSA. Ling et al. described the clinical and pathological features of six cases of “minimal change” MSA, noting that individuals with this variant had a shorter disease duration and more rapid disease progression [ ]. Induced Pluripotent Stem (iPS) Cell Models 6.1.1. Oligodendrocytes In 2015, Djelloul et al. first established iPS cells derived from patients with MSA [ ]. They generated iPS cells from fibroblasts of a healthy control and individuals with MSA-C and MSA-P, and differentiated these iPS cells into oligodendrocyte lineage cells to investigate α-Syn expression. Consistent with studies using the brains of patients with MSA [ , ], SNCA transcripts were detected in MSA-associated iPS cell-derived oligodendrocytes. α-Syn was detected in O4-positive-oligodendrocytes at 60 days in vitro (DIV) and localised to the perinuclear region from 65 DIV onwards. Although α-Syn expression persisted in oligodendrocytes until 110 DIV, its levels decreased in O4-positive oligodendrocytes over time. Azevedo et al. performed transcriptome analysis of oligodendrocyte lineage cells derived from fibroblast iPS cells of patients with MSA-P and MSA-C and healthy controls [ ]. Transcriptomic profiling of O4-positive oligodendrocytes at 130 DIV revealed positive enrichment of antigen presentation and processing pathways and negative enrichment of lipid metabolism in MSA-P and MSA-C cells. In addition, distinct biological processes were differentially enriched between MSA-P and MSA-C O4-positive oligodendrocytes; peptide biosynthesis and translation were predominant in MSA-P cells, whereas intracellular protein transport and protein targeting were enriched in MSA-C cells. These findings suggest that distinct molecular pathways underlie the early pathogenic mechanisms of different MSA subtypes. 6.1.2. Neural Progenitor Cells Using iPS cells derived from fibroblasts obtained from healthy controls and two patients with MSA-P, Herrera-Vaquero et al. differentiated iPS cells into neural progenitor cells to investigate early pathogenic mechanisms in MSA neurones [ ]. In the study, they examined α-Syn expression levels, mitochondrial alterations, and resistance to exogenous oxidative stress in neural progenitor cells from 7 DIV onwards. While SNCA mRNA expression levels were unchanged between the two groups, α-Syn protein was aberrantly translocated into the nucleus in neural progenitor cells derived from patients with MSA-P. In contrast to the intermediate mitochondrial morphology observed in control neural progenitor cells, the mitochondria appeared to be tubulated in cells derived from individuals with MSA-P. Additionally, compared with control neural progenitor cells, MSA neural progenitor cells produced more reactive oxygen species and underwent apoptosis. However, no difference was observed in the mitochondrial area or mitochondrial respiratory function between progenitor cells from individuals with MSA-P and controls. 6.1.3. Dopaminergic Neurones Compagnoni et al. generated dopaminergic neurones from iPS cells derived from the fibroblasts of healthy controls and patients with MSA-P or MSA-C [ ]. In their study, the levels of synapsin I (a synaptic marker) and tau protein (a neuritic marker) were significantly reduced in MSA dopaminergic neurones compared with the controls at 70 DIV. In contrast, α-Syn expression levels did not differ between MSA and control neurones at either 35 or 70 DIV. Furthermore, autophagic flux, as indicated by LC3-II levels, and lysosomal enzyme activities (α- and β-mannosidase) were decreased in MSA-affected neurones. In contrast to the findings reported by Herrera-Vaquero et al. [ ], decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity was observed in complexes II and III, accompanied by compensatory increases in the expression of these complexes. The expression levels of coenzyme Q (CoQ) 10 biosynthetic enzymes (all-trans-polyprenyl-diphosphate synthase 1 and 2, ubiquinone biosynthesis protein COQ4 homologue, and atypical kinase COQ8A) are also upregulated in MSA-associated dopaminergic neurones. Interestingly, autophagic and mitochondrial abnormalities differed between MSA subtypes and were more pronounced in MSA-P than in MSA-C-associated dopaminergic neurones. 6.1.4. Striatal GABAergic Medium-Sized Spiny Neurones Henkel et al. investigated how α-Syn accumulation leads to neurodegeneration in medium-sized striatal GABAergic spiny neurones generated from fibroblast-derived iPS cells [ ]. Although SNCA expression levels did not differ between MSA-P and control cells at 70 DIV, the fluorescence intensity of α-Syn in the cytoplasm and neurites was increased in MSA-P cells compared with controls. In contrast, electrophysiological and Ca 2+ imaging analyses have revealed significantly reduced excitability of medium-sized striatal GABAergic spiny neurones in MSA. Moreover, MSA-derived neurones released higher levels of α-Syn into the culture supernatant than control neurones, suggesting the acceleration of cell-to-cell propagation of α-Syn in MSA. Recently, Smandzich et al. performed a proteomic analysis using striatal GABAergic medium-sized spiny neurones derived from fibroblast iPS cells at 70 DIV [ ]. They identified significant alterations in 151 proteins in patients with MSA-P compared with the controls. Multiple analyses of oligodendrocytes, neural progenitor cells, dopaminergic neurones, and striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurones have demonstrated the involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and DNA damage responses in the pathogenesis of early-stage MSA. Regardless of the cell type examined, morphological and functional abnormalities of the mitochondria appear to be common features of early-stage MSA. Adult-Onset Proteolipid Protein (PLP) α-Syn Mouse Model of MSA Multiple transgenic animal models of MSA have been developed to elucidate its pathogenesis. However, a major limitation of the animal models that overexpress human α-Syn in oligodendrocytes is that disease-related changes occur from the time of fertilisation. To overcome the limitations of conventional transgenic animal models, Tanji et al. established an adult-onset, human α-Syn-inducible mouse model of MSA under the control of the PLP promoter using the Cre recombinase–loxP system [ ]. Along with the formation of toxic α-Syn oligomers, human α-Syn-positive GCI-like structures were observed, followed by the appearance of NCI-like structures. These GCI-like structures became proteinase K-resistant 50 weeks after human α-Syn induction. Consistent with the findings obtained from preclinical MSA cases [ , , ], human α-Syn was deposited in the perinuclear regions of neurones in the brainstem and putamen, although human α-Syn did not form fibrils in this model. Despite these similarities, this model also exhibits phenotypic features that are not typically observed in human MSA. Cognitive impairment occurs in approximately 37% of patients with MSA, generally at advanced disease stages, in conjunction with the classical triad of Parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction [ ]. In contrast, this mouse model displays memory impairment as early as 4 weeks after human α-Syn induction, followed by motor deficits 1 year later [ , , , ]. Recently, we performed a transcriptome analysis using the brains of this model [ ]. This revealed altered expression levels of transcripts encoding 10 vesicular transport and synaptic proteins, including synaptotagmin 13. Importantly, neuropathological and biochemical analyses of human MSA brains confirmed that the dysregulation of synaptotagmin 13 was caused by the accumulation of toxic α-Syn oligomers at synapses [ ]. Taken together, this MSA mouse model recapitulates some key aspects of the pathogenesis of early-stage MSA. 6.2.2. Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) Models Adult mouse, rat, and non-human primate models of MSA using viral vectors have been developed [ , , , , ]. In these models, AAV vectors were injected into the striatum of these models to induce human α-Syn in targeted cells and regions, thereby recapitulating the early stages of MSA. Williams et al. injected an oligotrophic AAV vector (Olig001-SYN) into the striatum of C57BL/6 mice to investigate the role of neuroinflammation in early MSA pathogenesis. Oligodendrocyte transduction by this vector in the dorsal striatum and corpus callosum led to demyelination with marked neuroinflammation [ ]. In the affected regions, resident microglia display increased major histocompatibility complex class II expression along with the infiltration of proinflammatory monocytes and CD4-positive T cells into the brain [ ]. In a subsequent study, the same research group demonstrated that interferon-γ secreted by CD4-positive T cells drives α-Syn–mediated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration [ ]. Given the increased numbers of HLA-DR-positive microglia in the putamen and substantia nigra of postmortem brains with MSA, these findings suggest that T-cell priming and infiltration into the CNS may contribute to the pathogenesis of early-stage MSA. Two types of rat models of MSA have been developed using the chimeric AAV1/2 vector carrying the human α-Syn sequence under the myelin basic protein MBP promoter [ ], or the Olig001 vector encoding human α-Syn [ ]. In the first model, GCI-like structures were observed in the striatum, substantia nigra, and corpus callosum [ ]. Neuronal loss occurred in the substantia nigra 3 months after AAV injection and in the striatum 6 months after injection. In the second model, GCI-like structures were similarly observed in the striatum, substantia nigra, and corpus callosum, as well as in the globus pallidus and thalamus [ ]. Non-human primate models have been established to further recapitulate the pathogenic processes of human MSA. AAV vectors have been injected into the putamen and caudate nucleus of rhesus macaques ( Macaca mulatta ) [ ] and into the putamen of cynomolgus macaques ( Macaca fascicularis ) [ ]. In the rhesus macaque MSA model, aggregated α-Syn was observed in oligodendrocytes within the caudate nucleus, putamen, and corpus callosum [ ]. Proteinase K-resistant GCI-like structures were formed in the striatum. This model also exhibited demyelination in the corpus callosum and striatum 3 months after the induction of human α-Syn expression. Consistent with the regional distribution of α-Syn, microglia were activated in the affected regions [ ]. Activated microglia have also been observed in the substantia nigra. In a cynomolgus macaque model, thioflavin S-positive GCI-like structures have been observed in the putamen [ ]. Similarly to the rhesus macaque model, microglia were activated in the putamen along with T cell infiltration. All genetically modified and AAV animal models of MSA are summarised in . 6.2.3. Inoculation Models Several species of abnormal α-Syn fibrils have been injected into the brains of transgenic and wild-type mice to investigate how pathological α-Syn propagates in vivo . Previously, A53T transgenic mice inoculated with brain homogenates from patients with MSA exhibited significantly increased levels of insoluble phosphorylated α-Syn and α-Syn oligomers compared with non-inoculated controls [ , ]. However, contrary to expectations, α-Syn aggregates developed predominantly in neuronal cell bodies and neurites, rather than in oligodendrocytes [ , ]. Similarly, inoculation of MSA brain homogenates into Tg (SNCA)1Nbm/J mice resulted in human α-Syn–positive aggregates largely restricted to neurons [ ]. Moreover, inoculation of MSA or PD brain homogenates into wild-type mice did not alter the proportion of α-Syn localised to oligodendrocytes. In contrast, two recent studies from Université de Bordeaux reported that a synthetic, thioflavin T-negative α-Syn fibril strain (1B fibril), assembled from human recombinant α-Syn, self-replicated and induced MSA-like pathology in mice [ , ]. Interestingly, 1B fibrils caused phosphorylated α-Syn-positive structures in the nucleus of primary mouse neurons [ ]. Injection of 1B fibrils into the striatum of wild-type mice produced phosphorylated α-Syn–positive neurites spreading along neuronal connectivity [ ]. These neurites became fragmented, contorted, and curled six months after inoculation, and importantly, both GCI- and GNI-like structures then emerged in parallel with these structural alterations [ ]. A structural analogy between the 1B fibril fold and the human MSA fibril fold was identified in one of the patients with MSA reported by Goedert et al. [ , ]. The 1B fibrils closed thioflavin T-binding pockets [ ], suggesting that such closed pockets may directly contribute to the formation of MSA-like pathology. Other Models Three major transgenic mouse models of MSA have been established, in which human α-Syn is overexpressed under the control of different oligodendroglial promoters, including PLP [ ], MBP [ ], and 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide 3′-phosphodiesterase, respectively [ ]. These models exhibit key pathological and clinical features of MSA, such as the formation of GCI-like structures, motor deficits, and autonomic dysfunction [ , , , , , , , , , , ]. However, α-Syn overexpression occurs from the stage of fertilisation, limiting their suitability for investigating the pathogenic processes underlying early-stage MSA. 7. Conclusions In the present review, we comprehensively summarised the current understanding of early-stage MSA. Notably, several shared features, such as mitochondrial dysfunction and specific neuroinflammation, consistently emerged in both the in vitro and in vivo MSA models. However, critical questions remain regarding whether these features reflect genuine pathogenic processes or are influenced by methodological differences and species-specific factors. In fact, both in vitro and in vivo models are designed to replicate some of the key features of early-stage MSA, based on the hypothesised sources and propagation pathways of abnormal α-Syn. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Care for patients with complex brain disorders (CBDs) is often fragmented across multiple brain-related medical specialities, resulting in diagnostic and treatment delays, duplication of services and inconsistent follow-up. While integrated care models exist in other areas of medicine, little evidence describes how patients experience interdisciplinary brain medicine clinics (BMCs) or what quality-improvement priorities should be addressed as these services develop. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study captures patient perspectives on the BMC, a novel interdisciplinary healthcare setting for patients experiencing CBDs in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Patient interviews and a survey identified three key themes influencing care quality: (1) Navigation and continuity, (2) Communication of diagnoses and plans and (3) The therapeutic alliance. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY The findings highlight specific, actionable quality improvement strategies for interdisciplinary brain healthcare clinics, including (1) Introducing a care navigator, (2) Providing structured after-visit summaries and preparatory materials and (3) Embedding empathy and communication training within the education of practitioners who will provide this care. Introduction Complex brain disorders (CBDs) are conditions characterised by overlapping symptoms across the domains of affect, behaviour and cognition (ABC). They encompass a range of disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias, Parkinson’s disease with psychiatric or cognitive features, traumatic brain injury or epilepsy with neuropsychiatric sequelae, and functional neurological disorders. CBDs are often managed in a siloed manner. Different brain-related specialists might each see the same patients, but understand and describe their presentations through the differing perspectives and language of their respective fields. Research increasingly shows that many brain disorders could benefit from integrated clinical approaches and medical education. While integrated clinical care models have proven effective in improving patient outcomes, care coordination and reducing healthcare costs, there remains a significant gap in the implementation of these models for managing CBDs. The Brain Medicine Clinic (BMC) at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre (SHSC) was established in 2020 to provide integrated interdisciplinary care for patients with CBDs. It serves as the flagship clinic of the Azrieli Brain Medicine Fellowship at the University of Toronto, a competency-based fellowship completed over 1–2 years that accepts fellows from neurology, psychiatry, geriatric medicine, physical medicine and rehabilitation, paediatrics and neurosurgery for integrated skill-building in the assessment and treatment of CBDs. The BMC is the core longitudinal clinical experience of the fellowship, acting as a “one-stop shop” for patients with CBDs by providing integrated interdisciplinary assessments and ongoing follow-up for brain-related symptoms ( ). Initially operating virtually from July 2020 to December 2024, the BMC transitioned to a hybrid model in January 2025, offering both virtual and in-person visits. The clinic sees adults aged 18 years or older with chief complaints involving at least two of the ABC domains who are likely to benefit from at least two brain-related specialities. It is based at a tertiary academic hospital in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA), but serves patients from across Ontario due to the specialised nature of its integrated interdisciplinary model. Typical patient cases include individuals experiencing overlapping disturbances in mood or emotional regulation, changes in personality or behaviour, and/or impairments in cognition such as memory, language or executive function. As outlined in , Brain Medicine fellows or residents complete the initial comprehensive evaluation, which includes a detailed clinical history, physical examination and bedside cognitive testing using standardised assessment tools. On the same day, fellows present the patient at interdisciplinary rounds attended by supervising staff neurologists, psychiatrists, physiatrists and a neuropsychologist. Ad hoc consultation with neuroradiology and neurosurgery is also available if there is a clinical need. The fellow then reconvenes with the patient to deliver the team’s integrated impressions and recommendations, which may include further work-up for diagnostic clarification, treatment adjustments, or referral to community support services. Follow-up visits are arranged as clinically indicated and patient care is transitioned back to the referring physician when deemed appropriate by the team. Although the BMC represents a novel model with potential to improve care for patients with CBDs, no prior studies have reported on the patient experience of attending this type of clinic. Understanding patient perspectives can provide valuable insights to help integrated interdisciplinary clinics effectively anticipate and meet the evolving needs of patients. This study used qualitative interviews and a patient survey to examine the experiences of individuals attending the BMC. Our objectives were to identify barriers and facilitators to care, highlight areas for improvement, and generate actionable quality-improvement priorities for the BMC, while also providing insights that may inform the design and replication of similar integrated care models for CBDs in other health-system contexts. Methods Study design This study used qualitative interviews and a structured survey to evaluate patient experiences at the BMC. It followed a concurrent mixed-methods design, with demographic questions completed at the start of the session, interviews conducted immediately afterward, and the patient experience survey completed at the end of the same session. Semi-structured interviews were guided by an interview framework developed collaboratively by a team of physicians, fellows and researchers from the clinic and used to explore patients’ expectations and clinic experiences. The structured survey included three sections: demographics, functional status and patient experience. The patient experience section included six 5-point Likert-type items (strongly agree to strongly disagree, plus N/A) assessing whether concerns were addressed, involvement in decision-making, provision of resources, willingness to recommend the clinic, barriers to accessing services and perceived helpfulness of navigation support, as well as a single global satisfaction rating (1=very unsatisfied to 5=extremely satisfied). See for the interview guide and survey. This project used the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s Model for Improvement, a framework for structuring quality improvement (QI) initiatives in clinical settings. It emphasises defining aims, identifying measures of improvement and testing change through iterative Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles. Consistent with the framework’s early diagnostic phase, this project focused on patient experiences and priority gaps in care at the BMC, providing a foundation for future PDSA cycles to test and refine interventions. Participants Patients who visited the BMC between May and July 2024 were recruited through voluntary response sampling. This sampling strategy was selected to include both new consults and follow-up visits, allowing for a comprehensive range of patient interactions with the clinic’s services. Eligible patients were contacted by the research team via email and phone. Of the 50 patients contacted, 15 consented to participate in the study. See for patient demographics. Patient and public involvement Patients and members of the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination of this research. Their contribution was limited to participation in interviews and surveys, which informed the findings and QI recommendations. Data collection Between July and August 2024, participants were invited to complete a 30 min interview conducted via Zoom. The interviews followed a semi-structured guide that allowed for in-depth discussions regarding participants’ pre-appointment expectations, experiences during the visit and outcomes thereafter. Two members of the research team (KS and JV) conducted the interviews to maintain consistency in data collection. Interviews were scheduled at the convenience of the participants, and all sessions were audio-recorded. Researchers administered a structured survey alongside the interviews, with demographic and health information collected at the start of each session and patient experience and satisfaction assessed at the conclusion. To preserve confidentiality, participants were not asked to disclose diagnostic details, and the research team did not access identifiable clinical records or protected health information. Participants received a $15 gift card as compensation for their time. All participants provided both written and verbal informed consent before their involvement in the study. Researchers determined that thematic saturation had been achieved after 15 interviews and recruitment was stopped. Thematic saturation was defined as the point at which no new codes, concepts or insights emerged during iterative review of interview transcripts. All audio files, interview transcripts and survey data were stored on encrypted institutional servers with access restricted to the study team. This project was conducted as a QI initiative at SHSC. In accordance with institutional policy, it was deemed not to constitute human subjects research, as the findings were intended to support programme feedback and clinical service improvement. Data analysis The audio recordings of the interviews were manually transcribed verbatim and analysed with NVivo. One research assistant (KS) performed inductive line-by-line coding to develop a coding scheme, which was then reviewed by the research coordinator (JV). Themes were identified from the codes through an iterative process following Braun and Clarke’s model of reflexive thematic analysis to ensure the findings were empirically grounded. The semi-structured format enabled interviewers to adapt the questions in response to participant narratives and allowed for the exploration of emerging concepts. Survey data were analysed descriptively to generate frequencies and proportions for each item. The survey and interview data were collected during the same session but analysed separately; the quantitative findings were then used to complement and contextualise the qualitative themes. Results Thematic analysis: factors contributing to quality of care Three main themes were identified as related to quality of care at the BMC: (1) Access, Navigation and Coordination, (2) Knowledge Translation and (3) Therapeutic Alliance. The results are organised and presented by theme, with representative patient quotations provided in and a visual summary provided in . Access, navigation and coordination Patients highlighted the systems and processes that shaped how they entered and navigated the BMC, often comparing these with their previous clinical experiences. This theme, referred to as access, navigation and coordination, encompasses three sub-themes: (a) Follow-up and continuity of care, (b) Coordination of care and (c) Accessing health services and information. Follow-up and continuity of care Patients’ experiences with BMC follow-up varied, with some reporting a lack of clarity about future steps within the clinic. Patients described frustration related to gaps in follow-up, with some feeling they had “fallen between the tracks” (Male, 80–84) and needed to proactively contact the clinic to ensure follow-through with their care plan. Several participants reported that limited communication from the clinic contributed to uncertainty about next steps and adversely affected their sense of continuity of care. Accessing health services and information Patients also described challenges in accessing health services and information, including referrals, community resources and online information, particularly among those with minimal external support or a lower functional status due to their complex conditions. As one patient explained, “The problem I came in with is part of the reason that I’m not getting the work done” (Female, 50–54). Patients who had support persons identified that they played a critical role in helping them overcome barriers to accessing recommended services and resources. Care coordination Despite these challenges, many participants still felt that care was more streamlined than in previous care settings. Participants appreciated the centralised approach to specialist care, especially given the complexity of their conditions. One participant observed, Instead of having to go from specialist to specialist, it’s more centralised. You have specialists who all communicate. I always felt like the other specialists would kind of just push me to the next one because they couldn’t figure it out. (Male, 25–29) These perspectives highlight the perceived benefits of the BMC’s integrated care model, with patients reporting experiences of more efficient and coordinated care compared with navigating multiple specialists independently. Knowledge translation Many patients described their experiences at the BMC as being shaped by how information from clinical encounters and overall clinic processes was communicated to them and their care partners. This theme, referred to as knowledge translation, also considered the extent to which patients’ expectations aligned with their experiences. Two sub-themes were identified: (a) Understanding of the encounter and (b) Understanding of the clinic. Understanding of the encounter Patients who clearly understood the discussions from their appointments typically reported a higher-quality and more positive care experience. One patient highlighted the importance of tailoring communication to meet individual patient needs and comprehension levels, stating, “I appreciated the fact that they explained things to me in my way that I could understand” (Male, 60–64), with other participants echoing this sentiment as well. Conversely, some patients reported feeling uncertain about their diagnoses, management options and subsequent steps following their appointment. Some patients described that reviewing their BMC consultation notes with their primary care provider helped answer their remaining questions and increased their understanding of the BMC’s impression and plan. One patient explained, I didn’t fully understand what they were telling me, but once my family doctor got the note and took me through the note, it kind of fell more clearly into place. (Male, 70–74) Access to written documentation, particularly when reviewed with another trusted clinician, helped some patients better interpret and contextualise the information discussed at their BMC visit. Understanding of the clinic Patients’ understanding of the BMC’s structure, processes and services was pivotal in their care experience. Those who were well-informed about the clinic’s interdisciplinary approach, care delivery methods and the extensive range of available services generally reported more positive and enriching encounters. One patient reflected, “It’s nice that there are multiple clinicians on the team where they can all deal with you at the same time”, demonstrating an understanding of the clinic’s purpose and operational flow (Female, 25–29). Participants whose experiences fell short of their expectations often expressed dissatisfaction. For

Therapeutic alliance Patients reported that their experiences at the BMC were strongly influenced by the degree to which they felt a trusting and collaborative partnership (ie, a positive therapeutic alliance) with their clinicians. Therapeutic alliance refers to the quality of the relationship between patients and clinicians, encompassing trust, rapport, empathy and collaboration. It includes the following sub-themes: how patients perceive their clinicians’ ability to (a) Adopt a person-centred approach, (b) Effectively address their needs and concerns, (c) Build rapport and trust and (d) Demonstrate key qualities desired in a healthcare professional. Person-centred approach BMC patients valued and emphasised the importance of being heard, respected and treated as active partners in their care. For instance, one patient mentioned that he valued the “back and forth in the conversation”, which made him feel involved rather than the professional “just providing information” (Male, 80–84). The majority of participants (n=9, 60%) reported feeling empowered and more satisfied with their care when they felt actively included as partners in the healthcare process. Addressing needs and concerns Three participants reported that their medical needs and concerns were not adequately addressed or validated, which they associated with less satisfactory experiences. For example, one participant stated that “it felt very much like – it’s like you could tell (BMC physician) hasn’t been through chronic pain” (Female, 25–29). Feeling unheard or misunderstood left patients frustrated and less confident in their clinician’s ability to offer meaningful solutions. Rapport and continuity Some participants (n=7, 46.7%) highlighted the importance of care continuity in building stronger connections with their physicians. As one participant explained, “I think because the last two appointments I’ve been seeing the same doctor, yeah, I feel like that built the rapport” (Female, 30–34). The therapeutic alliance was enhanced when participants felt they could trust their physicians and had the opportunity to build strong and collaborative relationships. Clinician qualities Nearly all participants (n=13, 86.7%) highlighted empathy, professionalism and knowledge as key clinician qualities. One remarked, “They all, every one of them, seemed compassionate and caring” (Male, 65–69). Active listening and effective communication skills were particularly impactful, with one participant stating, For a very long time, we talked about, you know, my history, my condition, things like that. They did not really cut me off, and they really listened. (Female, 45–49) Several participants (n=8, 53.3%) also emphasised the importance of clinicians’ knowledge and professionalism, expressing confidence in the specialised care they received. In contrasting their experience in the BMC with previous care, one participant stated: I think other specialists just kind of slapped a label on what was going on, and they didn’t do anything further… but I feel, with this brain clinic, that’s what they specialise in. And so I definitely trust this diagnosis. (Female, 50–54) Overall, the aforementioned clinician qualities were key to shaping patient experiences at the BMC. Contextual factor: virtual care environment Virtual care emerged as a significant contextual factor influencing how patients experienced accessibility and interpersonal connection at the BMC. Most patients (n=14, 93.3%) reported that the virtual format improved care accessibility by reducing travel time and associated costs. One patient highlighted these benefits: “Saving travel time and parking fees was good… and it can be confusing getting into a hospital and getting to the right place” (Female, 50–54). Some participants felt that the quality of virtual interactions matched that of in-person visits, noting that clinicians effectively built rapport and trust. For instance, a participant mentioned, “I don’t think that the fact that it was virtual deteriorated from the quality of the process” (Male, 70–74). Some participants even preferred virtual visits for the comfort and relaxed environment of their homes, which reduced stress and allowed for better interpersonal interactions. Additionally, some felt that virtual consultations did not facilitate as comprehensive an assessment as in-person visits. For example, one participant noted, “I guess a downside is that they don’t feel that they need to check… my sensation” (Female, 30–34), suggesting a perceived reduction in thoroughness. These findings highlight the multifaceted impact of virtual care on patient care quality. Satisfaction survey Survey findings reinforced the themes identified through the qualitative interviews. Most respondents (n=10, 66.7%) strongly agreed or agreed that their concerns were addressed when they met with the BMC physicians and/or neuropsychologist, while only one disagreed. Similarly, 90% of participants either strongly agreed or agreed that they felt included in decisions about their healthcare. When asked if the team provided information about resources or help they could access after their appointment, 66.7% either strongly agreed or agreed, while 13.3% disagreed. In terms of access, 46.7% of patients either strongly agreed or agreed that it was difficult to access recommended health services or resources, while 46.7% of participants disagreed or strongly disagreed with this statement. Most patients (n=12, 80%) strongly agreed or agreed that having someone connect them to community resources and programmes would have been helpful. The overall satisfaction with the BMC was high (mean score of 4.1/5), and 86.7% said they would recommend it to other people with similar needs or concerns. Full survey findings are detailed in . Discussion The results of this study demonstrate how access, knowledge translation and therapeutic alliance shape patient experiences at the BMC, with virtual care functioning as a key contextual factor. Patients valued the BMC’s centralised and interdisciplinary model of care. Many study participants perceived the BMC as more cohesive and efficient than reported experiences of fragmented care in other settings, consistent with evidence supporting integrated care for complex conditions. While overall satisfaction was high, the findings revealed meaningful opportunities for improvement, which have been synthesised into three main practice recommendations. First recommendation: care navigator Addressing the concerns participants raised about continuity of care and resource navigation is an area of opportunity in the BMC. Introducing a care navigation role represents a potentially feasible strategy to support care coordination and communication. Evidence from other chronic and complex care populations suggests that patient navigation programmes can improve care coordination and patient experience. Some studies in dementia care suggest that navigation may be cost-effective in select populations, particularly among individuals with higher care needs. These findings are based on relatively homogeneous patient groups and may not be directly transferable to the diagnostically and symptomatically heterogeneous population served by the BMC. As such, care navigation within the BMC is best framed as a QI intervention requiring context-specific evaluation of feasibility, resource implications and perceived value. A patient navigator was introduced to the clinic in September 2024, providing an opportunity to iteratively assess these factors using QI methods, with findings informing the refinement and sustainability of the role within an interdisciplinary brain medicine setting. Second recommendation: improved knowledge translation Patients valued clear and tailored explanations of diagnoses and treatment plans, while communication gaps often led to confusion and uncertainty. Improved knowledge translation is essential to better align patient expectations and clinical realities. We recommend the creation of a comprehensive website and preparatory package that clearly explains the clinic’s structure, interdisciplinary model and care processes. Online resources, including provider biographies and structured clinic information, have been found to reduce patient uncertainty, enhance satisfaction and facilitate informed decision-making. The introduction of an after-visit summary could reinforce key information discussed during consultations, provide clear follow-up instructions and ensure patients leave each visit with actionable steps. Although consultation notes are currently available for patients to review independently or with

We recommend the creation of a comprehensive website and preparatory package that clearly explains the clinic’s structure, interdisciplinary model and care processes. Online resources, including provider biographies and structured clinic information, have been found to reduce patient uncertainty, enhance satisfaction and facilitate informed decision-making. The introduction of an after-visit summary could reinforce key information discussed during consultations, provide clear follow-up instructions and ensure patients leave each visit with actionable steps. Although consultation notes are currently available for patients to review independently or with their primary care physicians, no written summary is provided at the conclusion of the visit. There is evidence to suggest that structured summaries can improve self-efficacy, support treatment adherence and aid in recalling medical instructions for patients managing chronic conditions. Collectively, these initiatives would strengthen patients’ understanding, foster engagement and enhance overall satisfaction throughout their care journey. These interventions could be implemented within the existing BMC structure but would require coordinated interdisciplinary input and upfront clinician and administrative time. Feasibility, effectiveness and sustainability should be evaluated through patient-reported experience measures and operational metrics as part of routine QI. Third recommendation: enhanced therapeutic alliance The therapeutic alliance between patients and clinicians is a well-established determinant of care quality and treatment outcomes. In our study, patients emphasised the importance of feeling heard, understood and respected. This reinforces findings in the psychiatric literature that effective communication and collaboration enhance engagement and satisfaction. Conversely, when communication was perceived as inadequate, or BMC physician or neuropsychologist recommendations were misaligned with patient expectations, participants described feelings of frustration, underscoring the role of interpersonal skills in maintaining a strong alliance. Given the complexity of the BMC’s patient population, strengthening the therapeutic alliance will likely improve care engagement and continuity. The Azrieli Brain Medicine Fellowship programme provides a structure to integrate intentional training in key relational competencies in the training of Brain Medicine specialists. We propose that this fellowship should include evidence-based strategies for empathy and compassion training (eg, use of role play and direct observation and feedback to teach active listening, validation and responsiveness to emotional cues) as a method to improve the patient experience. These interventions could be implemented incrementally using existing institutional web platforms and documentation systems without requiring additional clinical infrastructure. Their feasibility and perceived value could be evaluated through routine patient-reported experience measures as part of ongoing QI efforts, as well as through pre- and post-evaluation of fellows’ knowledge, skills and attitudes related to therapeutic alliance building following targeted educational exposures. Considering virtual care for brain medicine Participants described both benefits and drawbacks of virtual care. Many participants valued its convenience, reduced travel time and cost savings, particularly those living outside the GTA, from which the BMC frequently receives referrals. This aligns with prior research highlighting that virtual models can improve access, enhance comfort and reduce logistical barriers for patients with neurological conditions. However, challenges such as difficulty building rapport, distractions during consultations and perceived limitations in physical assessments were common participant concerns. Similar qualitative work has also shown that virtual platforms can enhance accessibility while introducing challenges related to privacy, technology and the relational aspects of care. The virtual care environment may not fully replicate the interpersonal and diagnostic depth of in-person visits, as certain observational and interactive components of care are more difficult to achieve virtually. This study’s findings reinforce the role of virtual care as a complement rather than a replacement for in-person care for patients with CBDs who may require interdisciplinary input and hands-on assessments. The American Academy of Neurology specifically recommends that the appropriateness of virtual visits be determined on a case-by-case basis to best support patient needs. While best practices for hybrid models remain underexplored in the literature, programmes such as the Virtual Behavioural Medicine programme in Toronto suggest that strategic integration of virtual and in-person care can improve patient outcomes while maintaining accessibility. Evidence suggests that virtual care models are most effective longer-term when they preserve fidelity to their intended purpose and outcomes, such as supporting clinical care delivery and access, while remaining adaptable to changing clinical contexts. With the BMC’s transition from a fully virtual to a hybrid model in January 2025, future research is needed to assess how this approach influences patient satisfaction, quality of care and continuity across specialities. Understanding when virtual visits are most beneficial, how they impact the therapeutic relationship, and whether they can effectively support long-term management of CBDs will be key to optimising the hybrid care model for this patient population. Study strengths Participants were broadly representative of the larger BMC population, as supported by demographic comparisons with a retrospective chart review conducted between May 2024 and May 2025 (manuscript being prepared for submission). to a hybrid model in January 2025, future research is needed to assess how this approach influences patient satisfaction, quality of care and continuity across specialities. Understanding when virtual visits are most beneficial, how they impact the therapeutic relationship, and whether they can effectively support long-term management of CBDs will be key to optimising the hybrid care model for this patient population. Study strengths Participants were broadly representative of the larger BMC population, as supported by demographic comparisons with a retrospective chart review conducted between May 2024 and May 2025 (manuscript being prepared for submission). To mitigate selection bias associated with voluntary response sampling, all patients seen in the clinic during the recruitment period were invited to participate, including both new consultations and follow-up visits, without restriction by diagnosis or symptom profile. Relative to the broader clinic population described in the chart review, participants may overrepresent individuals with higher educational attainment and those whose symptoms more significantly impacted their ability to work, while potentially underrepresenting patients with more marked cognitive impairment. These factors may limit the generalisability of certain findings. Methodological rigour was supported through the use of a standardised semi-structured interview guide, verbatim transcription and iterative coding reviewed by multiple team members. Interviewers did not have access to participants’ clinical records or diagnostic information, reducing the risk of interviewer bias and diagnostic anchoring and ensuring that analyses reflected participants’ lived experiences. The themes identified are consistent with existing literature on integrated care for complex conditions, supporting the plausibility and broader relevance of the findings despite these constraints. Limitations Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. Although broad recruitment was used to reduce selection bias, participation remained voluntary, and participants who chose to engage in the study may differ systematically from those who declined. This potentially over-represents individuals with more extreme experiences or those with greater capacity or ability for participation. The use of virtual interviews may have excluded patients with limited access to digital technology or lower digital literacy, potentially skewing the sample toward individuals with higher socioeconomic status or technological proficiency. Second, referral pathways to the BMC are not standardised; patients are initially referred to clinicians, who then determine whether they are seen in the BMC or an alternative setting. This variability introduces potential selection bias in the patient population and limits the external validity of our findings. Additionally, because the BMC operates using a symptom-based rather than diagnosis-driven model and serves a diagnostically heterogeneous population, traditional illness staging frameworks were not applicable. As a result, the study was unable to assess whether patient experiences varied by time since symptom onset or illness trajectory. Third, while thematic data saturation was achieved with 15 participants, our small sample size constrains the generalisability of our results and may not fully capture the heterogeneity of experiences within the broader BMC patient population. Additionally, without a formal saturation grid, external verification of saturation is limited. The small sample also limited our ability to conduct subgroup analyses to explore whether satisfaction or perceived quality of care differed according to patient characteristics. Fourth, patients were not involved in developing the interview guide or survey, which may limit the extent to which the tools reflect patient priorities. Additionally, the patient survey was developed specifically for this study and was not adapted from a validated instrument. While the items were designed to capture domains relevant to the BMC experience, the lack of established psychometric properties limits comparability with other patient-experience measures and may reduce measurement precision. Finally, the study focused exclusively on patient-reported experiences and omitted insights from BMC clinicians, care partners and administrative staff. This single-source perspective also limited methodological triangulation. The inclusion of additional data types or stakeholder perspectives would have likely enriched the analysis by providing a more comprehensive and multidimensional perspective of the clinic’s operations and patient outcomes. These findings should be interpreted within the context of the Canadian healthcare system. In Canada’s tax-funded, single-payer model, barriers to care are largely organisational, such as referral pathways, wait times and service availability. In this context, a multi-specialist consultation model like the BMC may help mitigate inefficiencies in referral pathways and reduce fragmentation of care. There may, however, be barriers to scaling such an integrated clinic for CBDs in health systems characterised by private or mixed provision, where affordability and insurance coverage play a greater role in shaping service design and provision. Conclusion This study provides meaningful insights into the experiences and perceptions of patients with CBDs at the BMC and sheds light on key factors that influence care quality, including access, navigation and coordination, knowledge translation and the therapeutic alliance. While patients expressed high overall satisfaction with the clinic’s interdisciplinary care model, the findings also highlight areas for improvement, particularly in follow-up processes, communication strategies and the integration

barriers to scaling such an integrated clinic for CBDs in health systems characterised by private or mixed provision, where affordability and insurance coverage play a greater role in shaping service design and provision. Conclusion This study provides meaningful insights into the experiences and perceptions of patients with CBDs at the BMC and sheds light on key factors that influence care quality, including access, navigation and coordination, knowledge translation and the therapeutic alliance. While patients expressed high overall satisfaction with the clinic’s interdisciplinary care model, the findings also highlight areas for improvement, particularly in follow-up processes, communication strategies and the integration of virtual care. Addressing these gaps through evidence-based recommendations, such as implementing a dedicated care navigator, enhancing patient education resources, providing high-quality medical education and adopting hybrid care models, may further improve the quality of care delivery within the BMC. These findings underscore the importance of continuous QI initiatives to ensure the clinic remains responsive to the complex and evolving needs of its patient population, including structured opportunities for teams to anticipate system needs and reflect on care processes. Future work using iterative PDSA cycles will be critical to evaluating the effectiveness and sustainability of proposed interventions and adapting them as needed. Further research is needed to include input from care partners, healthcare professionals and administrators to provide a more comprehensive perspective on the clinic’s operations and enable a holistic approach to enhancing care delivery. Building on these findings, the BMC has the potential to serve as a model for integrated care in managing CBDs and drive improvements in both patient outcomes and healthcare system efficiency. Introduction Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurones and the presence of hallmark motor symptoms, including resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability [ ]. It is evident that, in addition to motor manifestations, a significant proportion of patients (over 90%) experience non‐motor symptoms (NMS) that result in considerable impairment to quality of life and daily functioning. These symptoms encompass a wide range of conditions, including emotional disturbances (e.g. anxiety and depression), sleep disorders, cognitive impairment, pain and autonomic dysfunction. It is noteworthy that many of these symptoms can occur during the prodromal phase and have the capacity to affect psychological and physiological well‐being [ ]. Consequently, early recognition and effective management of NMS are critical for improving patient outcomes. Pharmacological therapy remains central to the management of PD, but it is often limited by adverse effects and suboptimal efficacy for NMS [ ]. It is evident that exercise has gained prominence as a significant adjunct strategy, with mounting evidence underscoring its benefits across multiple NMS domains, including mood, sleep, cognition, and pain [ ]. Contrary to previous reviews that offer broad narrative summaries or merely catalogue mechanistic findings, this review synthesises the highest‐level clinical evidence within each major NMS domain (accompanied by a cross‐domain summary), with the aim of enhancing clinical interpretability while minimising redundancy. Given the paucity of mechanistic evidence in this field, we propose a hypothesis‐driven peripheral–central framework to account for the convergent exercise‐related benefits observed across NMS domains. This framework also highlights key translational gaps (e.g. standardised NMS phenotyping and dose–response parameters) that constrain the precision of exercise prescriptions. The present study, therefore, examines the effects of exercise interventions on NMS in PD and discusses potential underlying mechanisms to inform clinical application and comprehensive disease management. 2. Methods This narrative review synthesised current evidence on the effects of exercise on NMS in PD. It also summarised preclinical findings solely in terms of biological context. In view of the considerable heterogeneity observed in study designs, exercise modalities, and outcome measures, it was determined that a narrative approach would be a more suitable form of analysis than a systematic review [ ]. A structured PubMed search was conducted from December 2015 to January 2026, with a focus on studies published in the most recent 5 years. Additionally, the reference lists of key reviews and clinical trials were screened. A comprehensive search strategy was employed, encompassing search terms such as ’Parkinson’s disease’, ’exercise/physical activity’, ’aerobic’, ’resistance training’, ’mind–body’, ’non‐motor symptoms’, ’depression/anxiety’, ’cognition’, ’sleep’, ’pain’, and ’autonomic dysfunction’. Eligible studies were human clinical investigations (meta‐analyses, randomised/controlled trials and cohort studies) reporting at least one NMS outcome following a defined exercise intervention; pilot or pre–post studies were included when higher‐level evidence was limited for a domain. A comprehensive review of the extant literature was conducted to inform mechanistic hypotheses, with the caveat that the findings could not be used to support conclusions on clinical efficacy. The evidence was then organised according to level of evidence, with meta‐analyses and randomised controlled trials given the highest priority, followed by controlled and observational studies and finally pilot studies. This evidence was synthesised by NMS domain and exercise modality/dose when reported. Given the narrative design and variability in interventions and endpoints, there is potential for selection and publication bias; many of the included trials are small and differ in blinding, adherence monitoring and outcome definitions, which limits cross‐study comparability. 3. NMS in PD: Definition and Temporal Course 3.1. Definition and Clinical Spectrum The neuropsychiatric, cognitive, sleep/circadian, autonomic and sensory manifestations encompassed by NMS in PD are not captured by classical motor diagnostic criteria. From a clinical perspective, NMS are frequently categorised into the following five distinct groups: (i) neuropsychiatric symptoms (e.g. depression, anxiety, apathy and hallucinations/psychosis); (ii) cognitive impairment; (iii) sleep and circadian disturbances (e.g. insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness and REM sleep behaviour disorder); (iv) autonomic dysfunction (gastrointestinal, urinary, cardiovascular, sexual and thermoregulatory symptoms) and (v) sensory symptoms including pain and fatigue [ , ]. In order to facilitate systematic recognition and reporting in research and practice, the development of structured screening tools such as the Non‐Motor Symptoms Questionnaire (NMS Quest) has been undertaken, with the objective of highlighting the breadth of NMS burden across disease stages [ ]. 3.2. Temporal Course of NMS The progression of PD follows a staged trajectory (preclinical → prodromal → clinical PD), and several NMS‐related features are explicitly incorporated into the Movement Disorder Society (MDS) research criteria for prodromal PD [ , ]. The early non‐motor manifestations that are most frequently reported include REM sleep behaviour disorder, hyposmia, constipation, mood disturbances and autonomic complaints. By contrast, cognitive impairment, complex pain phenotypes and more severe autonomic dysfunction often become increasingly prominent with disease progression and multisystem involvement [ , ].
